## Proposition 10.93
**Statement:** If an area be contained by a rational straight line and a third apotome, the âsideâ of the area is a second apotome of a medial straight line.

**Step 1.** Let the area AB be contained by the rational straight line AC and the third apotome AD. I say that the "side" of the area AB is a second apotome of a medial straight line.

**Step 2.** Let DG be the annex to AD, so that AG and GD are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, neither AG nor GD is commensurable in length with the rational straight line AC, and the square on AG is greater than the square on GD by the square on a straight line commensurable in length with AG. [D10.3.3]

**Step 3.** Apply to AC the square on AG, producing AH as breadth, and apply to AC the square on DG, producing KH as breadth. Since AG and DG are each incommensurable in length with AC, and AC is rational, the squares on AG and on DG are each incommensurable with the square on AC. But the square on AC is rational, so the squares on AG and on DG are each irrational, hence medial. [D10.1.3, D10.1.4] Therefore AH and KH, being the breadths produced when medial areas are applied to the rational straight line AC, are each rational and incommensurable in length with AC. [10.22]

**Step 4.** Since the square on AG is greater than the square on DG by the square on a straight line commensurable with AG, and AG and DG are commensurable in square only, by 10.17 if we apply to AG a parallelogram equal to the fourth part of the square on DG and deficient by a square figure, it divides AG into parts commensurable in length.

**Step 5.** Since AG : DG :: sq(AG) : rect(AG, DG), and since sq(AG) = AC * AH and rect(AG, DG) is related to the applied areas, consider that sq(AG) - sq(DG) = AC * (AH - KH) = AC * LH (where L is such that the area corresponding to AH minus KH gives LH). Since the square on AG is greater than the square on DG by the square on a straight line commensurable with AG, by 10.14, the corresponding breadths maintain this commensurability relationship.

**Step 6.** Now the square on AG is commensurable with the square on DG, since AG and DG are commensurable in square. [D10.1.2] Therefore AH is commensurable with KH. [10.11, 6.1]

**Step 7.** But AH and KH are each rational and incommensurable in length with AC (Step 3). And AH is commensurable with KH. Therefore AH and KH are rational straight lines commensurable in square only (since they are commensurable — and being rational lines incommensurable with AC, their commensurability with each other makes them commensurable in length). In fact, since sq(AG) : sq(DG) :: AH : KH [6.1, 10.11], and AG, DG are commensurable in square (so sq(AG) is commensurable with sq(DG)), AH is commensurable in length with KH.

**Step 8.** Since AG and DG are commensurable in square only, AG is incommensurable in length with DG, so sq(AG) is incommensurable with rect(AG, DG). [6.1, 10.11] But sq(AG) = AC * AH, so AC * AH is incommensurable with rect(AG, DG).

**Step 9.** Now rect(AG, DG) is irrational since AG and DG are rational and commensurable in square only, so rect(AG, DG) is medial. [10.21] Apply twice rect(AG, DG) to AC; let the breadth be MH. Since rect(AG, DG) is medial and AC is rational, MH is rational and incommensurable in length with AC. [10.22]

**Step 10.** Since AD = AG - DG, we have sq(AD) = sq(AG) + sq(DG) - 2 * rect(AG, DG). [2.7] Therefore the area AB = AC * AD, and sq(AD) applied to AC gives AH + KH - MH (that is, the breadth for sq(AG) plus the breadth for sq(DG) minus the breadth for 2 * rect(AG, DG)). But we need the side of the rectangle AC * AD, not the square on AD.

**Step 11.** Let us restart the construction more carefully. Apply the rectangle AC * AD to AC. Since AD is a third apotome, let AD = AG - GD where AG, GD satisfy the conditions in D10.3.3. Let the square on a straight line w equal the area AC * AD, so that w is the "side" of the area. We wish to show w is a second apotome of a medial straight line.

**Step 12.** Following the method of 10.91 and 10.92, let BG be set equal to AG (extending the line) so that DG is the annex, and bisect GD at E. Apply to AG a rectangle equal to the square on EG and deficient by a square; let this give AG divided as the rectangle AO * OG = sq(EG), with O a suitable point. By 10.17, since sq(AG) exceeds sq(GD) by the square on a line commensurable with AG, the segments AO and OG are commensurable in length.

**Step 13.** Equivalently, apply the area AC * AD to the line AC. By 10.56 (which handles the third binomial and yields a second bimedial), the structure of the third apotome mirrors that. Following Euclid's method for apotome propositions: set out a rational straight line AC, and let the third apotome AD have annex DG, with AG the whole. Apply to AC the areas: let sq(AG) = AC * AH and sq(DG) = AC * KL, so AH and KL are the breadths.

**Step 14.** Since AG, DG are rational and commensurable in square only, and each is incommensurable in length with AC: the squares sq(AG) and sq(DG) are medial (as in Step 3). Hence AH and KL, being each a medial area divided by rational AC, are rational and incommensurable in length with AC. [10.22]

**Step 15.** Since sq(AG) is commensurable with sq(DG) (AG, DG being commensurable in square), AH is commensurable in length with KL. [6.1, 10.11] So AH, KL are rational and commensurable in length, hence AH - KL is rational. But both are incommensurable in length with AC.

**Step 16.** Now sq(AG) - sq(DG) = AC * (AH - KL). Since AD = AG - GD, we have rect(AG, DG) relates to the configuration. By 2.5, rect(AG, DG) + sq(GE) = sq(AE) where E bisects AD (note: E bisects the segment from G to... let us use 2.7 directly): sq(AG - GD) = sq(AG) + sq(GD) - 2*rect(AG, GD). So AC * AD is not sq(AD).

**Step 17.** We proceed directly. Let the area be S = AC * AD, and let w be a straight line such that sq(w) = S. We need to construct w explicitly. Following Euclid's approach in 10.91-10.92: bisect DG at E, and apply to AG a rectangle equal to sq(EG) falling short by a square figure. By 10.17, since sq(AG) > sq(DG) by the square on a line commensurable with AG, the resulting segments are commensurable. Let this application produce the point H on AG such that AH * HG = sq(EG).

**Step 18.** Then by 2.5, AH * HG + sq(EG) = sq(half of AG adjusted)... Instead, apply the standard Euclidean construction: since sq(AG) > sq(GD) by the square on a line commensurable with AG, and GD is bisected at E, apply to AG a parallelogram equal to sq(EG) and deficient by a square. This determines points on AG. The segments AH, HG are commensurable in length. [10.17]

**Step 19.** Set out that rect(AH, HG) = sq(EG). Since DG is bisected at E, by 2.5: rect(DG, GD) + sq(EG) is related, giving us sq(EG) = sq(GD/2). Actually, DG bisected at E means EG = DG/2 and DE = DG/2. Now we apply to AG a parallelogram equal to sq(EG) = sq(DG/2) = sq(DG)/4, deficient by a square. By 10.17, AH and HG are commensurable in length.

**Step 20.** Now construct: let AN = AH and let o be a point such that sq(o) = AC * AN, and let p be such that sq(p) = AC * HG. Then sq(o) + sq(p) = AC * (AN + HG) = AC * AG. Also, o and p are incommensurable in square (since AN and HG are commensurable in length, and the construction yields lines related to medial areas).

**Step 21.** Since AN * HG = sq(DG)/4 (from Step 19), we get AC * AN * AC * HG = sq(AC) * sq(DG)/4, so rect(sq(o), sq(p)) in area terms: sq(o) * sq(p) = sq(AC) * AN * HG = sq(AC) * sq(DG)/4. Hence o * p = (AC * DG)/2 (taking the positive root), and 2 * rect(o, p) = AC * DG.

**Step 22.** But rect(AG, DG) is medial (since AG, DG are rational commensurable in square only) [10.21]. Therefore AC * DG: since AC is rational and DG is rational but incommensurable in length with AC (given in the third apotome definition), AC * DG is medial [10.21, as AC and DG are rational but incommensurable in length]. Hence 2 * rect(o, p) = AC * DG is medial, so rect(o, p) is medial.

**Step 23.** Now sq(o) + sq(p) = AC * AG. Since AG is rational and incommensurable in length with AC, the rectangle AC * AG is medial [10.21]. So sq(o) + sq(p) is medial.

**Step 24.** We need to show that sq(o) + sq(p) is incommensurable with rect(o, p). We have sq(o) + sq(p) = AC * AG and 2 * rect(o, p) = AC * DG. So (sq(o) + sq(p)) : 2*rect(o, p) = AG : DG. [6.1] Since AG and DG are incommensurable in length, AG : DG is a ratio of incommensurable magnitudes, so sq(o) + sq(p) is incommensurable with 2*rect(o, p), hence with rect(o, p). [10.11]

**Step 25.** Now sq(o) = AC * AN and sq(p) = AC * HG. Since AN and HG are commensurable in length (Step 18), AC * AN is commensurable with AC * HG [6.1, 10.11], so sq(o) is commensurable with sq(p). Therefore o and p are commensurable in square. [D10.1.2]

**Step 26.** Since sq(o) + sq(p) is medial (Step 23), o and p are not commensurable in square with a rational line in the standard sense; in particular, o and p are medial straight lines. Since sq(o) = AC * AN, and AN is rational (as shown: AN is commensurable with AH which is rational [Step 14-15]), sq(o) is the rectangle of a rational line AC and a rational line AN with AN incommensurable in length with AC. So sq(o) is medial [10.21], hence o is medial. Similarly p is medial.

**Step 27.** We have established: o and p are medial straight lines, commensurable in square only (since they are commensurable in square by Step 25, and incommensurable in length because if they were commensurable in length, sq(o) + sq(p) and rect(o,p) would be commensurable, contradicting Step 24), their sum of squares is medial (Step 23), and the rectangle contained by them is medial (Step 22), and the sum of squares is incommensurable with the rectangle (Step 24).

**Step 28.** Now w = o - p (since AD = AG - GD, and the construction mirrors the subtraction). We have sq(w) = sq(o) + sq(p) - 2*rect(o, p) = AC * AG - AC * DG = AC * (AG - GD) = AC * AD, confirming that sq(w) equals the original area. [2.7]

**Step 29.** Since o and p are medial and commensurable in square only, and they contain with each other a medial rectangle (Step 22), the remainder o - p is a second apotome of a medial straight line. [10.75]

**Step 30.** Therefore the "side" of the area contained by the rational straight line AC and the third apotome AD is a second apotome of a medial straight line. Q.E.D.

heath_proof_text: For let the area AB be contained by the rational straight line AC and the third apotome AD; I say that the “side” of the area AB is a second apotome of a medial straight line. For let DG be the annex to AD; therefore AG, GD are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, and neither of the straight lines AG, GD is commensurable in length with the rational straight line AC set out, while the square on the whole AG is greater than the square on the annex DG by the square on a straight line commensurable with AG. [X. Deff. III. 3] Since then the square on AG is greater than the square on GD by the square on a straight line commensurable with AG, therefore, if there be applied to AG a parallelogram equal to the fourth part of the square on DG and deficient by a square figure, it will divide it into commensurable parts. [X. 17] Let then DG be bisected at E, let there be applied to AG a parallelogram equal to the square on EG and deficient by a square figure, and let it be the rectangle AF, FG. Let EH, FI, GK be drawn through the points E, F, G parallel to AC. Therefore AF, FG are commensurable; therefore AI is also commensurable with FK. [VI. 1, X. 11] And, since AF, FG are commensurable in length, therefore AG is also commensurable in length with each of the straight lines AF, FG. [X. 15] But AG is rational and incommensurable in length with AC; so that AF, FG are so also. [X. 13] Therefore each of the rectangles AI, FK is medial. [X. 21] Again, since DE is commensurable in length with EG, therefore DG is also commensurable in length with each of the straight lines DE, EG. [X. 15] But GD is rational and incommensurable in length with AC; therefore each of the straight lines DE, EG is also rational and incommensurable in length with AC; [X. 13] therefore each of the rectangles DH, EK is medial. [X. 21] And, since AG, GD are commensurable in square only, therefore AG is incommensurable in length with GD. But AG is commensurable in length with AF, and DG with EG; therefore AF is incommensurable in length with EG. [X. 13] But, as AF is to EG, so is AI to EK; [VI. 1] therefore AI is incommensurable with EK. [X. 11] Now let the square LM be constructed equal to AI, and let there be subtracted NO equal to FK and being about the same angle with LM; therefore LM, NO are about the same diameter. [VI. 26] Let PR be their diameter, and let the figure be drawn. Now, since the rectangle AF, FG is equal to the square on EG, therefore, as AF is to EG, so is EG to FG. [VI. 17] But, as AF is to EG, so is AI to EK, and, as EG is to FG, so is EK to FK; [VI. 1] therefore also, as AI is to EK, so is EK to FK; [V. 11] therefore EK is a mean proportional between AI, FK. But MN is also a mean proportional between the squares LM, NO, and AI is equal to LM, and FK to NO; therefore EK is also equal to MN. But MN is equal to LO, and EK equal to DH; therefore the whole DK is also equal to the gnomon UVW and NO. But AK is also equal to LM, NO; therefore the remainder AB is equal to ST, that is, to the square on LN; therefore LN is the “side” of the area AB. I say that LN is a second apotome of a medial straight line. For, since AI, FK were proved medial, and are equal to the squares on LP, PN, therefore each of the squares on LP, PN is also medial; therefore each of the straight lines LP, PN is medial. And, since AI is commensurable with FK, [VI. 1, X. 11] therefore the square on LP is also commensurable with the square on PN. Again, since AI was proved incommensurable with EK, therefore LM is also incommensurable with MN, that is, the square on LP with the rectangle LP, PN; so that LP is also incommensurable in length with PN; [VI. 1, X. 11] therefore LP, PN are medial straight lines commensurable in square only. I say next that they also contain a medial rectangle. For, since EK was proved medial, and is equal to the rectangle LP, PN, therefore the rectangle LP, PN is also medial, so that LP, PN are medial straight lines commensurable in square only which contain a medial rectangle. Therefore LN is a second apotome of a medial straight line; [X. 75] and it is the “side” of the area AB. Therefore the “side” of the area AB is a second apotome of a medial straight line.
